## Ad Liska
Born: July 10, 1906 · Died: Nov 30, 1998 · Class of 1925
PCL Baseball Hall of Fame · Oregon Sports Hall of Fame

Liska was the first Nebraska baseball player to make it to the big leagues. He started as a teacher and semi-pro player, even making an appearance at the age of 19 for the Lincoln Links in 1926. His big league debut came for the Washington Senators in 1929. After five years of major league service, he bounced around and found another stop in Nebraska with the Omaha Packers in 1935.

The signing that would define his career came with the Portland Beavers AA team in 1936. He dominated the PCL circuit for the rest of his career, pitching for the Beavers from age 29 to 42, amassing 242 minor league wins with a 3.05 ERA.

Former player Dario Lodigiani, who faced Liska while Ad was in his 40s, said "I was so bad against Liska (in the PCL) that I think even if he had walked the ball up to the plate, I couldn't have hit him."

The enclosed cut signature came from the pictured PSA/DNA certified index card, bearing certification number L14850.

## Ray Prochaska
University of Nebraska - End

Prochaska was a part of the famous 1940 Cornhusker squad. After a thrilling but disappointing defeat to #1 Minnesota, the Big Red would rebound to rattle off eight consecutive victories.

Their performance brought the team national recognition and a first ever invitation to the prestigious Rose Bowl.

The tilt came against #2 Stanford, and the Huskers put up a mighty fight, ultimately falling 21-13 in front of 92,000 fans.

Prochaska would play in the NFL in 1941 with the Rams, before joining the service for World War II.

After the war, he served as an assistant coach for Nebraska and worked his way up to the NFL as a line coach and offensive coordinator. He would coach in the NFL for 28 years; an incredible achievement.

He was elected to the Nebraska Football Hall of Fame in 1986.

## Royal "King Kong" Kahler

Known as "King Kong Kahler", he played offensive and defensive tackle for the Huskers from 1937 to 1940, lettering his final three years.

The 1940 Huskers were in their 4th season under head coach Biff Jones. They were hungry for more after a 2nd place finish in the Big Six with a 7-1-1 record in 1939. The season opened with a close 13-7 loss to #1 Minnesota, but the Huskers bounced back and ran the table, winning eight in a row en route to a Big Six title and an invitation to their first ever bowl game.

The tilt came against #2 Stanford in the prestigious Rose Bowl, putting Nebraska on the map as a prominent college football team and gaining national recognition. The Huskers gave Stanford everything they could handle, before eventually falling 21-13. Nebraska finished ranked #7 in the nation and seemed destined for continued success, but the looming war would derail the program for many years until Bob Devaney was hired in 1962.

The Eagles selected Royal in the 1941 NFL Draft and he then reunited with his brother Bob with the Green Bay Packers in 1942.

Born: March 22, 1918
Died: Feb 21, 2005
Nebraska class: 1940

## Glenn Presnell
Nebraska Football HOF / 2x All-MVC / First Team All-American / NFL Champion / First Team All-Pro

Presnell was a dynamic threat all over the field throughout his career. He could run, pass, catch, and kick. His booming leg hit an NFL record 54-yard field goal in 1934, a mark that would stand for nearly two decades.

At Nebraska, Presnell was a halfback and quarterback on offense, while playing safety on defense. His efforts helped the Cornhuskers stun Red Grange and the Illini with a 14-0 defeat in 1925. In 1927, he would lead the nation in total yards gained and earned first team All-America honors.

Presnell's pro career began with the Ironton Tanks, before joining the Portsmouth Spartans (pictured on front) in 1931. He led the NFL in total offense in 1933 and set the record for most points scored in a season with 64.

The Spartans team didn't survive the Great Depression, and were purchased and relocated to Detroit to become the Detroit Lions. As fortune would have it, the Lions' owner asked Presnell and his wife to pick the team's new colors.

Presnell later recalled: "Mr. Richards, the owner, the day I was up there and signed my contract, he said: 'There's a table out there in the next office covered with uniforms. Why don't you pick out the colors you like?' I went out. My wife was with me. We saw this Honolulu blue and silver and we fell in love with it."

In 1935, Presnell would lead the Lions to their first NFL Championship. Those colors he chose would stand the test of time in Detroit and are still featured to this day.

Born: July 28, 1905
Died: Sept 13, 2004
Nebraska class: 1927
Honors: Nebraska Football HOF, 2x All-MVC, First Team All-American, NFL Champion, First Team All-Pro

## Rex Hudler
Kansas City Royals - Broadcaster

On May 13, 2014, the Royals were tied 1-1 with the Rockies when the broadcast opened the bottom of the 4th with a zoomed in shot of the moon.

Broadcaster Ryan Lefebvre quipped that they were obligated to showcase the moon when Rex Hudler quickly added that he agreed and "it's a beautiful planet!"

There was an awkward pause before Ryan added: "... well it's a moon..."

Hudler, still enthralled, doubled down with "well it looks like a planet to me!" and added that "School Day at the K" was coming up.

Ryan quickly offered that "maybe they can cover the whole: star, planet, and moon concept."

Rex, always a good sport, laughed and took his verbal slip in stride.
